headline: Found that repurchase hazard halves by day 60 and designed a one-time-buyer audience as a budget reallocation, not a new-customer play
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I ran the first RFM workstream of the client's LTV brief: quantified when first-time buyers of the wellness line stop repurchasing, sized the audience by pack size, and designed the DSP audience and its A/B test.
metrics: 32% of the wellness line's buyers over five years bought exactly once
36% of first-time buyers did not repurchase within 365 days; by pack size the rate ranged from 29% to 68%
Daily repurchase hazard peaked at days 22-30 and fell to 47% of peak by day 61, setting the cut-off at 60 days
163 products mapped to pack-size bands with a mapping QA that reconciled detail rows to control totals

detail.overview: The client's brief asked for a retargeting audience of first-time buyers who churn. I reframed it as two questions — from which day does repurchase stop, and how many such people exist now — and answered with AMC retail-purchase history, a hazard-rate view of the first-to-second purchase gap, and a 14-day repurchase curve by pet, form, pack size and order quantity.
detail.problem: The brief's privacy threshold was wrong by 20x, timezone handling shifted monthly counts, pack sizes were mis-mapped from truncated product names and shipping-case notation, an overlap check against the existing loyalty line-item ignored its own exclusion rules and had to be thrown out, and slide denominators confused the internal reviewer.
actions: Corrected the brief (audience minimum, timezone) and built discovery queries for coverage, identity, left-censoring and product mapping
Chose the churn cut-off from the hazard-rate drop rather than a cumulative-curve percentile and cross-checked it against a platform reference
Dropped a bag-depletion segmentation after measurement showed it flat, and re-cut by pet type instead
Merged the professional sub-line into the wellness line (163 products), fixed pack-size mapping and re-ran the repurchase curve until the unmapped share was resolved
Loaded results to BigQuery with assert-based QA (row sums, detail-to-control totals, mapping counts) and built four slides with explicit numerator/denominator labels

Designed the audience rule (exactly one order, past the drop-off point, no second order, refreshed daily), its exclusion from the existing loyalty line, and a randomized A/B test over the seasonal sale
impact: Designed the audience and test plan; audience creation and the A/B run were not yet started at the end of the log
Reframed the story for the client: value comes from reallocating existing retargeting budget to the hesitation window, not from new reach

headline: Turned 4,700 overlapping audience segments into a defensible expand/exclude plan: pet segments ~3x CVR, exclusion sized by reach loss not count
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I analysed which Amazon audience segments an AI-driven DSP prospecting line item actually converts on, and designed the expansion/exclusion actions so they would not cannibalise high-value users — owning AMC SQL, BigQuery, the Python pipeline and the client slides.
metrics: Median user belonged to 122-124 segments at once, so segment-level ranking needed a peer baseline and a 20% coverage cap
Untargeted pet segments converted ~3x the segment average (2.8x dog / 3.1x cat) while the recommended 'Beauty' theme sat at ~1x
Naive name matching said 8-9 of the top 10 were already targeted; segment-ID ground truth corrected this to 6-7 of 10
Segment-level budget sums overstated the bottom-10 share (22.7%) versus user-level de-duplication (19.4%)
The AI optimiser dropped high-performing pet segments 1.2-1.9x faster than weak broad ones as the campaign paced down

detail.overview: The prospecting line item had no explicit targeting; Amazon's AI chose audiences. I pulled segment-level impressions and conversions from AMC, loaded them to BigQuery, and built a Colab pipeline (control totals, tiered asserts, EDA, gating, de-duplication, ground-truth join, daily allocation trends, user-level exclusion curves) ending in a Tufte-style two-slide client deck with speaker notes.
detail.problem: Users belonged to ~140 segments each, so simple sums double-counted, converters inflated any campaign-level baseline by ~1.2-1.3x, identical segment names mapped to different IDs, and the largest segments could never show high CVR by construction. Excluding weak segments risked removing users who also sat in strong ones, and 'savings' framing was wrong because the campaign budget was fixed and re-allocated daily.
actions: Replaced a composite score with plain CVR plus narrative, at the account lead's request, and gated segments on minimum impressions and conversions
Re-based the CVR index on the peer average and then dropped the index entirely for percentage CVR the client could read
Rejected name-based matching after finding one-to-many name-to-ID mappings, and joined against actual matched segment IDs from sibling line items to decide what was truly untargeted
Derived a statistical ceiling (segment CVR <= campaign CVR / coverage) to justify a 20% coverage cap and separate 'do not touch' mega-segments

Tested the vendor's 'Beauty' recommendation: broad Beauty was average with ~3.5x the pet NTB cost, only narrow Beauty sub-segments beat average, so they were seeded as audience signals for a 4-week split test rather than promoted
Normalised daily segment trends against the campaign's own pacing and sized the exclusion by a user-level reach-loss budget with absolute NTB guardrails
impact: Delivered an expand/exclude recommendation with quantified reach and conversion trade-offs per species, framed as redirection with guardrails rather than savings
Exposed that most 'top' segments were already targeted by sibling line items, redirecting the story from discovery to overlap reduction
Exclusion depth and split test were designed; live results after console changes were not yet measured in the log

headline: Validated a 365-day purchaser exclusion: new-to-brand share +9pt on DSP vs +1pt on the untouched control, NTB cost per unit halved
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I designed and ran the before/after measurement of a DSP targeting change amid Prime Day, a 64% budget cut and a trial-pack mix shift, and delivered the client slides and workbook.
metrics: DSP new-to-brand share 24.6% -> 34.0% (+9.4pt) vs Sponsored Ads control +0.9pt; difference-in-differences +8.5pt, consistent across three campaign-cut definitions
NTB units per unit of spend roughly doubled (+99%) across DSP+SA and nearly tripled on DSP alone (+186%)
NTB cost per unit -50% combined, -65% on DSP; DSP went from 74% more expensive than SA to 23% cheaper
Untreated loyalty line retained ~71% of purchases on a 67% budget cut, ruling out a market collapse
Excluding a discontinued trial pack lifted the DSP NTB gain from +9.4pt to +13.5pt, so the headline used the conservative figure

detail.overview: The client had excluded 365-day purchasers from DSP targeting to push new-to-brand acquisition and asked whether it worked. I built a gated AMC discovery series, chose comparable 21-day PRE/POST windows around Prime Day with a 7-day truncated attribution applied to both, used Sponsored Ads (targeting unchanged) and the loyalty line (not excluded) as controls, loaded everything to BigQuery with control-total asserts, and produced a two-slide client story plus internal appendix and a 14-sheet workbook.
detail.problem: Spend fell 64% between periods, so every absolute NTB metric was negative and the first slide read as failure. Attribution lag, a sale event on the exclusion date, a trial pack that made up 75% of one line's new purchases before disappearing, and a simultaneous audience change on one line all confounded the read.
actions: Chose conversion-time windows that avoid sale periods and applied the same truncated attribution to both, framing Prime Day carry-over as a conservative bias against the treatment rather than a wash
Set NTB share as the primary judgement metric with a directional DiD against Sponsored Ads and a market-demand check on the loyalty line
Replaced the all-negative absolute KPIs with a two-panel slide: absolute totals as context, NTB units per unit of spend as the conclusion, and moved NTB cost to a per-unit basis
Decomposed the efficiency gain into media price and conversion-rate components to pre-empt the 'it only improved because you spent less' objection
Isolated the trial pack by ASIN allow-list after price and keyword rules both failed, and produced a defence slide for the line whose NTB share collapsed
Enforced control totals with grain-aware tolerances and a balanced campaign panel
impact: Delivered a validated, conservative headline the client team could defend, with the sensitivity cases in speaker notes rather than on slides
Separating the concurrent audience-waterfall effect from the budget cut remained an open item pending budget stabilisation

headline: Proved an audience waterfall cut multi-line overlap from ~50% to ~34%, then expanded it with 22 measured segments and a video control group
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I validated an exposure-based audience de-duplication cascade across DSP awareness line items, found why it saved no budget, and designed the full console spec for adding untargeted dog/cat segments in size order with a measurement plan.
metrics: Users reached by 2+ line items fell from 49.9% to 33.8% (-16pt) after the waterfall
Cost per unique user -39%, of which ~26% was media-price deflation, leaving ~13-15% as the cascade's own effect
AI prospecting line's first-touch share rose from ~50% to ~71% once overlap was removed
Estimated tier positions were 3-4x off actual coverage for one health segment, so every tier was re-ordered on measured coverage
An intersection audience designed as AND actually reached 76k users against a 14k ceiling, proving it ran as OR

detail.overview: A cascade where each upper tier excludes the users it has already exposed had been live on display line items for two months. I measured whether it hit its three goals (less duplicated reach, lower spend, better cost per unique user), then found untargeted catalogue segments for both species, sized them on a common denominator, placed them in tier order with parent-child rules, and wrote the console-ready before/after spec with segment IDs, QA checklist and a display-vs-video difference-in-differences plan.
detail.problem: First measurement used within-line frequency and read the cascade as a failure; the correct grain was cross-line overlap. Identical segment names mapped to different IDs, the planning sheet disagreed with the live console, on-site and off-site segment lists had drifted apart, and an intersection audience (parents x pet owners x cat food) was silently running as a union and cannibalising lower tiers.
actions: Re-specified the validation as cross-line overlap, exposure time-gap distribution and first-touch tier order, all on a stable identity type
Separated the cascade's effect from a concurrent 26% media-price drop and a uniform budget cut, concluding it created a savings opportunity but did not execute one
Rejected a proposal to throttle the AI prospecting line and instead promoted its top discovered segments to explicit tiers with audience signals
Measured coverage of every candidate segment on one denominator, ranked tiers ascending, merged a near-duplicate large segment, and put child segments above parents
Proved the AND-vs-OR structural bug from matched-segment reach and put the affected lines on hold pending a rebuilt intersection
Unified on-site and off-site lists, scoped video line items out as a control, took a pre-change baseline and resolved 76 of 91 segment IDs via a single metadata query with explicit NOT logic
impact: Confirmed the cascade should not be rolled back and gave the team a defensible internal verdict
Delivered the execution spec for 22 new segments and 8 new line items; post-change effect is scheduled for measurement three weeks after go-live

headline: Proved OTT reached 18% of total audience no other Amazon channel touched, and killed a false 2.2x lift before it reached the client
context: For a premium coffee brand (Japan) I built the AMC-to-BigQuery-to-Python pipeline and the slide deck measuring what Prime Video and Fire TV ads added on top of DSP display and Sponsored Ads, then handled the local team's Q&A.
metrics: OTT-only reach = 52% of OTT reach and 18% of total unique reach across five Amazon media
100% of connected-TV impressions came through OTT; 80% of OTT impressions were CTV; 22% of OTT impressions were zero-cost bonus inventory
Fair comparison: OTT + display + search converted at 0.44x the display + search-only rate, replacing a contaminated 2.2x claim
Exclusive reach share by medium: Prime Video 46%, Fire TV 35%, display 58%, Sponsored Ads 56%

detail.overview: The client had run Prime Video and Fire TV campaigns on the agency's recommendation. I designed a user-level media-combination query (mutually exclusive combo partitions with a 14-day exposure envelope), loaded control totals and the master table into BigQuery, produced the slides in matplotlib, and iterated the narrative with the account lead and the Japanese team.
detail.problem: Campaign IDs arrived corrupted by Excel float rounding, product classification by price was wrong in both directions, a Fire Tablet placement hid inside display, and the first purchase-rate story compared OTT users against a baseline polluted by low-intent single-channel users, producing a plausible but false 2.2x lift.
actions: Replaced campaign-ID joins with campaign-name and supply-source tagging after proving the IDs returned zero rows
Cross-checked product ASINs on the live marketplace and hard-coded a prefix allowlist instead of a price threshold
Built a single combo-grain master query with control-total checks that reconciled to manual estimates within 0.04%
Reconciled five mutually exclusive exposure groups against the master totals and corrected the lift claim to 0.44x, reframing OTT as a prospecting layer rather than a converter
Added a volume slide (donuts and a three-way split of OTT-only reach) and proved combination reach was deduplicated and that the analysis measured co-exposure, not path order
Rewrote every headline with explicit denominators and corrected three factual errors in the presentation script before delivery
impact: Delivered a defensible four-slide deck plus appendix and a Q&A record the Japanese team used with the client
Prevented a false lift figure from reaching the client and established the rule that reach can be called incremental but purchases only 'OTT in the mix' without a holdout

headline: Audited Amazon's official path-to-conversion query template and found 11 defects before it touched client data
context: For a premium coffee brand (Japan) I turned a past AMC aggregation bug into a fixed SQL operating standard, then used it to audit and harden Amazon's official Path-to-Conversion instructional query before running it on the client's instance.
metrics: 11 defects identified in the official template (3 critical: alias/source-column collisions, an integer division that would zero out conversion rates)
Hardened query passed a 15-point self-check (no alias collisions, explicit CAST/NULLIF, COALESCE after LEFT JOIN, fixed identity type)

detail.overview: An earlier AMC query had returned wrong aggregates because column aliases reused source column names in a multi-CTE UNION ALL pipeline. I wrote down the root cause as an operating standard (forbidden alias list, prefix pipeline, explicit casting, staged validation queries, pre-submit checklist) and then applied that standard to Amazon's official Path-to-Conversion by Campaign Group template.
detail.problem: The official template reproduced the same bug pattern: aliases identical to source columns, a CTE named after a column, integer division in the off-Amazon conversion rate, SELECT *, non-sargable ARRAY_CONTAINS filters, first-conversion timing mixed with full-window revenue (overstated ROAS), no identity-type filter, and a paid-feature dependency.
actions: Documented the root cause of the earlier aggregation bug and codified a forbidden-alias list, raw_/u_/agg_/final_ prefix pipeline and a standard CTE template
Audited the official instructional query line by line against that standard and ranked 11 issues by severity
Rewrote the on-Amazon and off-Amazon versions with prefixed aliases, CAST/NULLIF ratios, COALESCE after LEFT JOIN, a fixed identity type and a sargable VALUES-based campaign-group map
Designed three pre-flight validation queries (campaign mapping, identity coverage, conversion-table scope) and an alternative first-conversion-only CTE to test the ROAS overstatement
Built matplotlib chart templates (top-N path bar, touchpoint-position mix, Sankey) with a PPT-safe export helper
impact: Designed a reusable AMC SQL standard that was later folded into a workflow prompt suite for all clients
Execution against the live instance and the three validation queries were still pending at the end of the log

headline: Redesigned a 180-line-item Amazon DSP audience stack into a reach-ordered exclusion waterfall before Prime Day, fixing two ladder faults found in live reach data
context: Full-funnel DSP audience and suppression architecture for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan); I owned the AMC measurement, the waterfall design and the activation handoff.
metrics: Four new AMC audiences measured at only 2.8-4.3% net-new reach against active purchase lines, so they were repositioned as budget-steering tiers rather than reach expansion
Pet-owner identity segment found 1.6x (dog) to 7x (cat) larger than the keyword line that was excluding it, a fault that would have driven that line's reach toward zero
Purchase ladder re-sequenced by measured reach: a brand-store retargeting line of ~3-5K users moved from rank 7 to rank 4

detail.overview: Ahead of Prime Day the client wanted its DSP audience settings optimized across Awareness, Consideration, Purchase and Loyalty for two product lines and two species. The work grew from placing four new AMC audiences into a full re-architecture: which audiences to build in AMC versus natively in the console, how each line item should exclude the tiers above it, what lookback windows to use, and how to order tiers so budget flows to the most valuable users first.
detail.problem: New audiences overlapped heavily with lines already running, so adding them would not add reach; console exclusion semantics (displayed as AND, executed as OR-removal) were being misread; several ladder positions were set by intent strength rather than audience size, so large tiers were starving small ones; and the activation team needed a document in exact setting names rather than analyst shorthand.
actions: Measured net-new reach and a 5x5 overlap matrix in AMC across all enabled line items, then re-scoped the new audiences from reach expansion to value-based budget steering

Split builds by capability: catalog in-market/lifestyle bundles as native console OR-includes (live, auto-refreshed), AMC only for custom event logic (high-value, NTB high-value, cart-not-purchase, trial-not-purchase, purchaser lookalike)

Set lookbacks from purchase cycle: 90-day purchaser exclusion on purchase lines (a 30-60 day repurchase cycle makes 180 days a win-back dead zone), 180-365 days for identity signals, and a no-recent-purchase exception stack for high-value tiers
Validated ladder order with June impression and unique-reach data per line item, removed a superset segment from a lower tier's exclusions and re-ordered the purchase ladder ascending by reach
Added species-level ASIN filters to the AMC audience queries after finding dog and cat versions returned identical users
Rewrote the activation handoff in verbatim setting names with before/after tables, plus a context log recording why each rule exists
impact: Delivered the full waterfall design, exclusion-stack definitions and AMC query package for activation; live results are tracked in a separate case
Established reusable rules: exclude by saved audience not segment lists, never exclude across species/line/inventory, order ladders by size and use intent only for budget weighting
Documented the console's exclusion semantics so future audits do not misread AND-notation as intersection

headline: Built a Prime Day 'hot lead' AMC audience (14-day product views, no purchase in 365 days) and designed a contamination-aware before/after read of the new exclusion waterfall
context: Prime Day activation and post-event measurement for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) on Amazon DSP; I proposed the audience logic, wrote the AMC SQL and built the measurement chart pipeline.
metrics: Audience defined on the platform's official 365-day new-to-brand rule instead of a lifetime window, keeping the segment buildable and comparable
Pre-event week showed detail-page views down 18% while CTR rose 13%, a signal read as spend-driven rather than demand-driven

detail.overview: Ahead of Prime Day the week-over-week report showed shoppers browsing but deferring purchase. I proposed targeting users who viewed the brand's product pages in the last 14 days but had no purchase in 365 days as a high-intent, likely new-to-brand audience at the top of the purchase waterfall, then designed how to judge whether the re-sequenced waterfall improved CPA once the sale distortion was removed.
detail.problem: A 'no purchase' rule risks including existing customers waiting to repurchase; the first query used a non-existent column; after go-live the audience delivered almost nothing for hours; and any post-event comparison is contaminated by pre-sale demand suppression, sale-period demand spikes and the 14-day attribution lookback.
actions: Wrote species-specific AMC rule-based audience queries (recent detail-page viewers LEFT JOIN 365-day purchasers, anti-join) and corrected the date column against the schema after a console error
Aligned the exclusion window to the platform's rolling 365-day new-to-brand definition rather than a lifetime window
Triaged zero delivery by eliminating causes in order (minimum size, match rate, refresh, sync latency up to 48h, bid level) and held observation after a bid increase instead of rewriting the audience
Tagged the daily series into clean baseline, pre-sale suppressed, sale, high-risk and low-risk post-sale windows and compared only clean baseline vs low-risk stabilised
Built a 7-day moving-average CPA / NTB CPA / NTB share chart with change-point markers and shaded contamination windows for the client deck
impact: Audience live before Prime Day; delivery normalisation and the measured CPA effect were still pending at the end of the log
Designed a reusable event-contamination framework for reading any setting change around a major sale

headline: Reframed a 'new-to-brand sales are falling' brief into 'units +30%, AOV -17%, DSP-to-search channel shift' and traced the root cause to line-item audience overlap
context: Monthly NTB deep-dive and nine-slide client storyline for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan); I owned the AMC SQL, BigQuery/Python analysis, visuals and slide narrative reviewed by my manager.
metrics: NTB sales +8% May to June with units +30% and AOV -17%, validated by ASIN-level totals within 0.3-0.7% of the headline query
Wellness line: DSP-attributed NTB sales -23% while Sponsored Ads +74%, read as channel shift rather than DSP failure
Awareness line items shared 47% of users off-site vs 4% for loyalty; multi-funnel-stage reach only 17-20% of exposed users
Configured vs delivering line items matched 96%, ruling out dormant settings as the cause

detail.overview: The client believed new-to-brand sales were declining. I decomposed May vs June NTB into units and average order value, broke it down by channel, product line, species and funnel, built ad-type and funnel-level path-to-conversion views, measured how many users actually travel across funnel stages, and quantified user overlap between line items to explain why.
detail.problem: The premise was wrong (total NTB grew; only DSP-attributed sales fell while search grew), aggregation thresholds blanked 7.5% of revenue when sliced too finely, path-level sales carry attribution bias, the official path template did not de-duplicate repeated funnel nodes, and several intuitive cannibalisation metrics turned out to have no valid basis.
actions: Split reporting into a low-dimension headline query and a high-dimension diagnostic query, and reconciled headline totals against ASIN-level sums
Grouped conversion paths at ad-type level, ranked by volume with CPA alongside, and switched the unit of analysis from orders to units for low-price trial products
Replaced exposure-joined channel totals with direct sums from the attribution table after spotting double counting
Rebuilt the path query to collapse each user to first-seen per funnel stage before sequencing, then verified zero self-repeats across four datasets
Measured line-item overlap as the share of users hitting two or more line items per funnel, separately on-site and off-site, and checked configured vs delivering line items
Dropped three metrics and one narrative link that could not be defended, re-ran the funnel-reach view on DSP plus search, and rewrote the story in neutral, channel-shift framing
impact: Nine-slide storyline delivered and accepted after manager review, with next steps prioritised (audience mutual exclusion in awareness and consideration, trial ASIN focus)
Showed the frequency-cap cut on loyalty had not reduced overlap, redirecting the fix toward audience exclusion design
Established a reusable QA cell (self-repeat check and touch-count distribution) for future path analyses

headline: Proved an OTT-retargeting line item reached 17-35% of its target cohorts vs 0.03% of control and lifted awareness impressions per member 2.2-2.7x (DiD)
context: Fixed-cohort difference-in-differences in AMC SQL for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan); I designed the cohorts, corrected the frequency metric and ran a line-by-line review of the v3 query.
metrics: Retargeting reach rate 17.5% (FTV cohort), 29.6% (PVA), 34.8% (both) vs 0.03% in the clean control group (roughly 550-1,100x)
Awareness impressions per cohort member rose 1.75-2.16x post-launch while control fell to 0.79x, a ratio-of-ratios DiD of 2.2-2.7x
Frequency among already-reached users rose +6.4% (PVA) and +7.5% (both) even in the diluted metric; control -2.0%

detail.overview: A retargeting line item was launched inside the awareness display campaign to re-expose users who had seen the brand's OTT (Fire TV / Prime Video) campaigns. The client questioned whether any observed effect was just 'more touches'. I built a fixed-cohort DiD in AMC to measure whether the line item reached the intended cohort and whether it added reach or frequency.
detail.problem: The first read said 'reach doubled, frequency unchanged'. The frequency metric averaged over everyone reached, so the many newly reached low-frequency users diluted it, hiding the lift among users who were already exposed. A follow-up line review of the v3 query also found that pre-window contamination by the retargeting line would go undetected, that campaign-name tokens could fabricate a 'both OTT' segment, and that the control group was selected on addressability while the treatment groups were not.
actions: Fixed the cohort before launch (OTT exposure up to the cutoff), split late-OTT users out of control, and measured identical 10-day pre/post windows
Isolated the retargeting line directly by line-item pattern instead of inferring it from aggregate frequency, after the team confirmed the naming convention
Switched the primary KPI to impressions per cohort member (reach x frequency) and treated frequency-among-reached as a dilution diagnostic
Reconciled the output with control totals (RT + other impressions = total post impressions) on every segment

Reviewed v3 line by line: added pre-window guard columns, a pre-flight naming audit, an addressability axis for the DiD, an extended console window for rolling-lookback audiences, and a placebo pre-period design
Withdrew a 'back-calculated' frequency table once I confirmed its inputs were assumed, and replaced it with assumption-free bounds
impact: Established that the retargeting line executed as designed (near-zero control leakage) and that its effect was mainly new reach plus a measurable frequency lift
Reframed the launch as a budget reallocation from broad prospecting to OTT-exposed users, making the real question 'was the reallocation worth it in NTB terms' for the path analysis
Designed the guard, placebo and variance additions needed before the DiD is reported; re-run still pending

headline: Built a full-year sales and cost estimate by ASIN objective group when the seasonality multiplier could not be measured, exposing it as a single explicit assumption instead of a hidden one
context: H2 forecast and ASIN-group performance reporting for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan), requested by my manager; I owned the sheet formulas, the AMC SQL and the Python/Excel estimation pipeline.
metrics: ~200 ASINs mapped into 9 objective groups with one spreadsheet formula (brand -> species -> life-stage / condition)

Estimate structured as 207 actual days plus 158 remaining days with one user-set H2 multiplier; NTB share method shown to be mathematically identical to the daily-average method under a common multiplier

detail.overview: Management wanted the year estimated as 'H1 actual NTB ROAS times remaining spend' for each product objective group, then asked to include July and the second-half sales events. That required a clean group mapping, a de-duplicated AMC query with halo sales in the advertiser's timezone, and a transparent extrapolation method.
detail.problem: DSP has no ASIN dimension so per-group spend can only cover Sponsored Products/Display with an ASIN match (brand video ads are structurally excluded); the first query used UTC dates and excluded halo sales, leaking revenue between sibling groups; and the platform retains 13 months, so the prior year's first half needed for a measured seasonality ratio no longer existed, while the warehouse held only campaign-level data.
actions: Wrote a LET / nested IF / REGEXMATCH sheet formula to assign each ASIN to an objective group, flagging the one dual-species SKU
Built the AMC query on a single attribution table for automatic de-duplication, with halo-inclusive totals, advertiser-timezone dates and an explicitly labelled 'Sponsored Ads only' spend column
Tested three routes to a measured seasonality multiplier (prior-year halves, campaign-level monthly trend, internal media plan) and documented why each was unavailable or out of scope
Parameterised the estimate: daily average of 207 actual days x 158 remaining days x one H2 multiplier, with NTB revenue via H1 NTB ROAS and NTB units via H1 NTB share
Generated a four-sheet workbook (assumptions, raw input, calculation detail, final estimate) with a disclaimer that the multiplier is a judgement, not a measurement
Recommended 'CY' over 'FY' to avoid fiscal-year misreading for a Japanese client
impact: Delivered a reproducible estimation workbook; the multiplier value and final figures were pending management sign-off
Made the spend coverage limitation (search only, ASIN-matched) explicit in the column name so the client cannot misread it as total spend

headline: Built a full-funnel penetration framework in AMC whose trend endpoints reconcile exactly to totals, revealing two under-invested funnel stages
context: Executive reporting for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan); I designed the AMC SQL, the cumulative logic, the BigQuery/Python visual standard and the client-facing investment diagnosis.
metrics: Awareness reach at ~70% of the defined pet-owner universe for both species lines, meeting the client's 70% benchmark
Purchase stage >90% ad-exposed share vs Consideration ~46-51% and Loyalty ~39-43%, identifying the two stages below the 70% benchmark
Last-period cumulative value matched the overall total for all 4 stages after redesign (previously off by up to 2.3 pp)

detail.overview: The brand runs Amazon DSP across Awareness, Consideration, Purchase and Loyalty for two product lines (wellness / therapeutic) and two species. Leadership asked how deeply each stage penetrates its audience and whether each stage is adequately funded against a 70% reach benchmark.
detail.problem: Awareness (reach over a segment universe) and lower-funnel stages (ad-exposed share of converters) needed different denominators yet one consistent chart set; the AMC instance only retained 13 months; the ASIN column used for product mapping was populated only on purchase events; and an initial version showed quarterly trend endpoints that did not match the overall pie.
actions: Defined stage-specific penetration metrics with aligned naming and a shared species split, and fixed the analysis window to the instance's 13-month retention
Mapped conversions to product lines via the item-level column populated on every event type after diagnosing why the ASIN column dropped two stages entirely
Rebuilt both queries as cumulative-to-period-end with a single shared cutoff so the final trend point equals the overall total by construction
Wrote an internal AMC SQL rule set (alias prefixes, JST timezone, CAST/NULLIF division) and a reusable prompt after alias-collision and timezone bugs recurred
Standardised a matplotlib visual guide (brand palette, donut + trend, 16:9 slide sizing, transparent SVG) and an in-memory RAW workflow for notebook reproducibility
Translated the results into a neutral-tone investment diagnosis: which stages exceed or miss the 70% benchmark and three reallocation options
impact: Delivered a reconciled 4-stage x 4-segment chart set (overall + monthly cumulative trend) used in the client's funnel investment discussion
Identified Consideration and Loyalty as below-benchmark stages and Purchase as saturated, framing a reallocation plus audience-expansion recommendation
Rule set and prompt were reused as the standing system prompt for subsequent AMC sessions

headline: Derived stage-specific DSP frequency caps from 13 weeks of AMC data, validating the global 2x awareness cap and recommending a ~70% cut to the loyalty cap
context: Frequency strategy for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) across Awareness, Consideration, Purchase and Loyalty; I designed the KPI logic per stage, the AMC SQL and the client slides.
metrics: Awareness: weekly frequency 2 reached ~78% cumulative reach vs a 70% target and was the modal answer in 9 of 13 weeks
Loyalty: subscription conversion rate at frequency 1 was ~11x the rate at frequency 25 for both product lines, with ~60% of subscribers converting organically
Consideration: users at weekly frequency 6 averaged ~2 campaigns vs ~1 at frequency 3, proving the 'cap leak' was cross-campaign overlap, not a query error

detail.overview: The client wanted to know whether the global frequency caps (2x/7d awareness, 3x/7d consideration, 25x/30d purchase and loyalty) are optimal for Japan, using different KPIs per stage: reach and cost per reach, CTR and detail-page-view rate, purchase rate, and subscribe-and-save rate.
detail.problem: Efficiency per frequency bucket rises monotonically because heavy users self-select, so 'best bucket' logic always removes the cap. AMC does not support window frames or standalone ORDER BY. Cumulative rates dip at the cap boundary because volume piles up there. A budget-reallocation simulation failed repeatedly in AMC. Ad-exposed purchase and subscription shares were initially misread as ad effectiveness.
actions: Aligned the analysis unit to each cap's period (13 clean weeks; two clean 30-day windows) and excluded sale weeks and the unfinished attribution week
Replaced bucket-level efficiency with cumulative-reach saturation: the minimum weekly frequency reaching 70% of reach, voted across weeks
Rebuilt cumulative metrics with a self-join because AMC rejects window frames, and exported raw counts for ratios
Diagnosed the consideration-stage spike at frequency 6 with a users x campaigns query, then anchored the cap recommendation to a penetration target to avoid circular logic
Adopted one KPI per stage with a ranked table (purchase rate; subscription rate from the all-conversions feed rather than digital-subscription fields)
Reframed high ad-exposed shares as potential cannibalisation and recommended a hold-out test for the purchase stage
impact: Confirmed the global awareness cap with local data and provided a per-stage recommendation set: keep 2 (awareness), test lower (consideration and therapeutic purchase), cut 25 to 5-7 (loyalty)
Consolidated four stages into one narrative for the client: reduce over-exposure and move budget to new-user acquisition
Left the budget simulation explicitly as a spreadsheet estimate with stated assumptions rather than an AMC result

headline: Proved that users reached by both discovery video and retargeting display convert new-to-brand ~6.7x more than retargeting alone, and redesigned the awareness audience stack around it
context: Awareness strategy for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) answering three client questions on reach sufficiency, frequency and budget; I designed the AMC SQL, the exclusive-reach and frequency methodology, the synergy test and the execution plan slides.
metrics: Every awareness channel exceeded its media-plan target on exclusive reach (107% to 504%), shifting the question from reach to efficiency
Users exposed to both discovery and retargeting channels showed a NTB conversion rate ~6.7x the retargeting-only group and ~4.5x the discovery-only group
Weekly frequency 2 was the only level where detail-page-view, purchase and NTB rates all rose together; a proposed cap increase was withdrawn
Top-priority audience line converted NTB at ~5.7x the rate of the catch-all pet-owner line, setting a measured top-down priority order

detail.overview: Six awareness placements (display, brand-plus, streaming TV, video ads, online video, sponsored awareness) ran with a weekly cap of 2. The client asked whether reach was sufficient against the media plan, what to recommend, and how to allocate budget; I added three supporting questions on optimal frequency, NTB-based allocation, and why users were seen up to 25 times despite the cap.
detail.problem: Exclusive reach had two competing definitions; the first frequency query pooled 13 weeks and used UTC columns, producing a reversed conclusion for streaming TV; AMC attributes last-touch so awareness NTB is under-counted; the cap leak was initially misdiagnosed as a settings error; and the audience lines were nested supersets with no explicit retargeting relay between discovery and display.
actions: Computed exclusive reach as users with channel breadth = 1 via a self-join, verified with identity checks, and replaced a share-of-total metric with cost per exclusive reach
Measured media-plan target achievement on exclusive reach for the four plan buckets
Rebuilt the frequency response curves as weekly rates averaged over 13-14 weeks in advertiser timezone, with weeks-observed as a reliability flag, and cross-checked DPV against purchase and NTB rates
Explained the cap leak as per-line order-level caps over overlapping audiences, confirmed high-frequency users were high converters, and chose to keep it rather than force an advertiser-level cap
Ran an NTB synergy test labelling users as discovery-only, retargeting-only or both, then extended the window and re-ran

Measured NTB rate per audience line and species, derived a top-down OR-NOT priority order, and drafted AMC retargeting audiences for streaming-TV and video-exposed users with exclusions on all prospecting lines
impact: Client approved increased discovery (streaming TV / video) budget; the plan adds a display retargeting relay that did not previously exist
Withdrew a cap-increase recommendation before it reached the client after multi-KPI validation
Delivered a global-team slide set with an explicit disclaimer list (selection bias, last-touch floor, currency reconciliation pending)

headline: Turned a retargeting scare into proof that it works: capture rate 78% at 3 months, and traced a 36% species overlap to shared audience segments
context: DSP audience diagnostics for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) under client escalation; I wrote the AMC SQL, redefined the metric and audited the targeting setup.
metrics: Awareness-to-Consideration capture rate rose from ~48% (1-month window) to ~78% (3-month window) once retargeting lag was included
Species overlap fell from ~36% of Awareness reach to under 1% at the Loyalty stage, confirming separated targeting deeper in the funnel
8 overlap queries reconciled exactly (segment sums equal total reach) before visualisation

detail.overview: The client wanted to know whether dog and cat campaigns reach distinct users across four funnel stages, and, after a low first read, whether DSP retargeting from one stage to the next was actually set up correctly.
detail.problem: A proven overlap query failed twice in AMC (root cause: a '+' in campaign names broke IN-list parsing). The first retargeting metric divided overlap by the upper-stage reach, making healthy retargeting look like 7-8%; a single-month window also ignored multi-week retargeting lag. The species overlap at Awareness (~36%) needed a root cause, not just a number.
actions: Rebuilt eight brand x stage overlap queries on LIKE-pattern matching and moved ratio maths outside AMC for parser safety
Verified every result with the identity cat_only + dog_only + both = total, then visualised as brand-coloured Venn strips with fixed-denominator (100%) shares
Redefined the retargeting metric as capture rate (overlap over the lower-stage reach) to answer the client's actual question
Re-ran the funnel-overlap query over three months to include lag and compared 1-month vs 3-month capture rates
Audited the live audience settings and found the same pet-owner segment reused across dog and cat lines plus duplicated segment IDs in the cat list
Designed a cross-channel (DSP awareness x sponsored 'General') overlap query using UNION ALL plus a single GROUP BY dedup
impact: Client-facing wording changed from 'is retargeting broken?' to evidence that roughly four in five lower-stage users had been reached upstream
Reframed species overlap as evidence of good separation deeper in the funnel, with a concrete fix for the shared awareness segment
Established a 3-month window and capture-rate definition as the standard for retargeting checks

headline: Built an 8-level auto-classification and daily KPI pipeline for 170+ sponsored-ad campaigns with zero unmapped rows, after catching a wildcard bug that had faked earlier passes
context: Reporting infrastructure for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan); I designed the AMC SQL taxonomy, the QA loop and the KPI joins.
metrics: 176 campaigns classified into brand x species with 0 unmapped; 68 in-month campaigns fully classified on funnel with no 'Other'
6 false 'Auto' classifications eliminated and a stage count corrected from 15 to 6 after replacing the separator
Residual unresolved cases reduced to 7, all traced to naming conflicts requiring owner confirmation rather than logic gaps

detail.overview: Every sponsored-ad campaign (products, brands, display, TV) needed spend, impressions, clicks, CTR, units, CVR, sales, ROAS and NTB by day, broken down by brand line, species, funnel, ad type, strategy theme, sub-theme and campaign - with the rule that no campaign may fall into 'Other'.
detail.problem: Campaign names followed three different conventions (pipe-delimited, underscore-delimited, funnel-first). The legacy query used bare substring matching, so a name containing 'SDA' was read as the wellness line; SQL LIKE treats '_' as a single-character wildcard, so using it as a token separator silently matched 'cat' as the 'Auto' tactic; cost was truncated by integer division; and cost-only or conversion-only campaigns dropped out of the join.
actions: Normalised campaign names into '#'-delimited tokens (pipes, spaces, underscores, brackets and plus signs) so LIKE matches are exact token boundaries
Ordered CASE rules per column by narrowest-first priority (e.g. therapeutic before wellness to protect 'SDA', Strategic before Competitor) and kept two funnel columns separate on purpose
Cast spend to DOUBLE before scaling, took impressions and clicks from the traffic table rather than the attribution table, and used FULL OUTER JOIN with COALESCE so every campaign appears
Wrote a companion QA query that flags any campaign landing in Other/UNMAPPED at any level and re-ran it after each rule change
Reconciled populations across columns (same 68 in-month campaigns on each) and hand-checked all 70 in-month campaigns for the sub-theme column
Escalated the 7 genuinely ambiguous names to the campaign owner in Japanese instead of guessing a rule
impact: Delivered a classification that reconciled to zero unmapped rows at brand, species and funnel levels on live data
Exposed that earlier 'passing' checks were invalid, preventing a silently wrong monthly report
Query became the base for a scheduled BigQuery refresh in the following workstream

headline: Rebuilt 10 AMC retargeting audiences with a 365-day no-purchase rule aligned to Amazon's NTB definition; 8 of 10 met the size floor
context: AMC clean-room audience build for a global PC brand (Japan) via its agency; I owned the SQL design, timezone logic, NTB alignment and the Japanese client reporting.
metrics: 2 audience categories x 5 lookback windows (30/60/90/180/365 days) = 10 rule-based audiences
8 of 10 audiences generated; the two shortest cart-based windows failed the minimum-size threshold
Purchase-exclusion window fixed at 365 days (Amazon NTB definition) independent of the intent window
400+ ASIN catalogue mapped in a reusable CTE

detail.overview: Two AMC segments the brand's DSP relied on (add-to-cart non-purchasers across organic and ads; Sponsored Ads clickers who did not purchase) had stopped delivering for lack of volume. The agency asked whether a lapsed segment can be revived and, if not, to rebuild them at 30/60/90-day recency for a new-to-brand acquisition campaign.
detail.problem: AMC has no concept of reviving an audience, and 'non-purchaser' is only judged inside the API time window that pre-slices every table, so a 30-day audience silently allowed buyers from 31+ days ago back in. The brand's KPI was NTB, which Amazon defines as no brand purchase in the prior 12 months. Add-to-cart and purchase live in a UTC-only table while the advertiser reports in JST, and Sponsored Brands clicks carry no creative ASIN.
actions: Answered the agency's revival question strictly from AMC documentation (refresh stops after 100 days unlinked, deactivation 30 days later) after separating documented mechanics from my assistant's interpretation
Standardised a reusable 400+ ASIN CTE and an anti-join pattern (LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL) over the full-signal conversions table for cart-adds and the Sponsored Ads traffic table for clicks

Split the design into an intent window (30 to 365 days, variable) and a purchase-exclusion window fixed at 365 days so every remaining user would count as NTB if converted, and dropped the ASIN constraint on exclusion to work at brand level
Applied a two-stage date filter: a sargable coarse prune on the UTC date column plus a precise JST boundary via CONVERT_TIME_ZONE_FROM_UTC, keeping the coarse edge one day outside the precise edge
Hand-checked every window boundary and corrected three off-by-one errors before submission; widened the API time window to 365 days plus buffer so the SQL exclusion was not truncated
Reported results in Japanese, explaining why the two shortest windows failed and proposing 180/365-day audiences as a delivery-rate vs intent trade-off
impact: 8 of 10 audiences generated and handed to the agency with documented logic
Designed the exclusion so that the audience is NTB-eligible by construction rather than by post-hoc filtering
Left Sponsored Brands click coverage and post-launch performance explicitly open

headline: Showed that removing a DSP frequency cap halved CPM but raised cost per reach 9% and cut reach 26%, recommending the cap be reinstated
context: Amazon DSP awareness campaign for a premium Scotch brand (Japan); I designed the pre/post test and wrote the AMC SQL.
metrics: Average frequency roughly doubled (4.3 to 8.5) over the same 14-day window after uncapping
CPM fell 44% while cost per unique reach rose 9% and unique reach fell 26%

detail.overview: The monthly 6x frequency cap on a DSP awareness line was removed to see whether the full funnel would improve. The cap had been lifted for all audiences at once, so no concurrent control group existed.
detail.problem: Without a hold-out, any comparison risks seasonal and accumulation bias; frequency naturally accumulates with window length, and AMC's aggregation thresholds return NULLs for thin buckets. Early queries also failed on a reserved-word alias and returned nothing due to a wrong year and a UTC timestamp column.
actions: Framed the test as equal-length 14-day pre (capped) and post (uncapped) windows to neutralise frequency accumulation
Chose cost per unique reach as the decision metric for an awareness objective, since it self-normalises across different budgets
Grouped frequency into five buckets and exported raw counts for spreadsheet ratios to avoid threshold NULLs
Diagnosed empty results with a discovery query on actual campaign and line-item strings before editing filters, then fixed the year and advertiser-timezone column
Computed frequency, CPR and CPM per line item and period and derived the change rates
impact: Concluded that cheaper impressions were absorbed by repeat exposure rather than new reach, and recommended reinstating a cap
Left the cost currency unit and one line item's missing pre-period data explicitly flagged as unresolved rather than reporting them as settled

headline: Proved top-20 paths cover 85% of reach, then built a composite-score view so low-budget premium video paths were not hidden
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I rebuilt the AMC path-to-conversion pipeline, fixed two silent metric bugs and produced a volume Sankey plus efficiency scorecard deck to assess premium video (Brand+/Fire TV/Prime Video) budget.
metrics: Top 20 of 6,510 paths covered 85.3% of reach; top 12 covered 80%; single top path covered 50%
Top-ranked single-touch awareness path alone accounted for ~52% of top-20 reach and was invisible in the Sankey
Premium video formats were ~10% of budget [REVIEW: basis not in log]

detail.overview: Rebuilt an Amazon Marketing Cloud path-to-conversion query for one brand instance (campaign-name priority grouping, unclassified campaigns excluded), loaded results to BigQuery and built in Colab a Plotly volume Sankey (top 20), a Pareto check, a composite efficiency scorecard (CPA, NTB CPA, CPR, ROAS, NTB ROAS; min-max normalised, weighted 1.0/1.5/1.0/1.0/1.5) with minimum-sample filters, and first-touch channel pivots for a three-slide client story.
detail.problem: Two silent bugs: 'users that purchased' equalled reach because the conversion CTE counted detail-page views and hard-coded a flag; and aliases named like source columns made the AMC parser read the raw column, producing purchases=0 with sales>0. Analytically, the playbook's volume-ranked top-20 Sankey hides low-budget premium video paths (volume trap), and single-touch paths cannot be drawn in a Sankey at all.
actions: Diagnosed the reach-equals-purchasers anomaly and split purchased_flag (purchases>0 or NTB purchases>0) from engaged_flag (DPV/clicks), adding users_engaged and a QA rule users_that_purchased <= reach
Traced impossible metric combinations to alias/source-column collisions and established a prefix naming convention (raw_/u_/conv_/imp_/sum_) plus MAX-based user de-duplication
Ran a Pareto analysis on all paths to justify the top-20 cut before presenting it
Kept the volume Sankey as the standard view and moved efficiency ranking to a separate composite-score table, with the client-specified weights and minimum reach/purchaser filters
Separated single-touch paths into a bar chart and clarified whether node percentages were within-step or overall
Rejected a Markov-chain attribution step because the AMC path is ordered by first exposure, not a true event sequence
impact: Delivered a validated three-slide structure (volume Sankey / efficiency scorecard / first-touch channel KPIs) for the premium video budget discussion
Designed the composite scorecard and QA rules; final score values and the corrected Fire TV query re-run were not yet verified in the log

headline: Reconciled an AMC channel dashboard to the ad console: cost within ~0-5% per channel, a -10.5% sales gap accepted after proving channel rankings unchanged
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I built and debugged a 19-version AMC SQL that unifies DSP and sponsored ads into console-equivalent channel KPIs, and defined when AMC numbers can be trusted.
metrics: Channel classification matched the console's 8 sub-funnels 1:1 after moving video detection to campaign-name keywords
Total product sales gap -10.5% (NTB sales -2.8%); ROAS ranking identical between console and AMC for all channels except one streaming format
A misclassification had hidden 100% of video sales inside awareness (+8.4% inflation) before the fix

detail.overview: Combined dsp_impressions and sponsored_ads_traffic (cost/traffic) with attributed events by traffic time (conversions) in two CTEs joined on channel, classified campaigns with a priority CASE (video, Brand+, Prime Video, Fire TV, bonus/awareness, consideration, loyalty, purchase; search ads separate), and compared every channel's cost, sales, NTB sales and purchases with console pivots.
detail.problem: Early versions used non-existent columns, a creative_type filter that never matched (all video sales fell into awareness), and a conversion-time table that dropped most sales. Even after fixes, a systematic -10.5% sales gap remained with no confirmed cause, raising the question of whether AMC efficiency KPIs could be used at all.
actions: Set AMC UI date range wide and filtered the exact analysis period in SQL, after realising the UI range and the WHERE clause act independently
Rejected the attribution-window hypothesis with data: AMC was below console for every channel except one, which a longer console window cannot explain
Dropped creative_type entirely and put a campaign-name 'video' rule at the top of the CASE so video and awareness can never double count
Corrected NTB column naming (new_to_brand_total_*) and video metric names against the schema reference
Compared ROAS and CPA rankings side by side and confirmed order was unchanged despite absolute gaps
Adopted a governance rule: absolute values from the console, relative channel efficiency from AMC
impact: Final query adopted as the channel performance dashboard with channel mapping validated against the console
Established a documented trust rule for AMC vs console KPIs; root cause of the residual sales gap left open

headline: Measured true incremental reach of Fire TV at 38.5% after removing search-ad retargeting noise, and validated funnel retargeting flows of 75% / 52% / 63.5%
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I designed AMC overlap queries by brand line, pet type and funnel stage, built pairwise Venn visuals and a slide/script set to test Amazon's 'unique reach' claim for streaming video.
metrics: Fire TV pure incremental reach 38.5% of its audience vs DSP awareness (61.5% overlapped); vs all other awareness channels: Prime Video 48%, Fire TV 42%, Brand+ 25%
Retargeting flow validated: 75% of consideration reach came from awareness, 52% of purchase from consideration, 63.5% of loyalty from purchase
Brand-line overlap ~18% of total reach; therapeutic line exclusive reach 8.7% vs 23% budget share; pet-type overlap ~50%

detail.overview: Replaced Amazon's parameter-driven overlap template with rule-based campaign grouping (keyword cascade in SQL) so new campaigns classify automatically, then ran three overlap analyses (brand line, pet type, funnel stage incl. streaming formats) with mutually exclusive exposure groups and distinct-user reach. Visualised in Colab with matplotlib-venn and python-pptx and wrote the client script in English and Japanese.
detail.problem: An initial read suggested Fire TV was 62% incremental, which was actually its overlap share. Including search ads polluted the picture because purchase/loyalty campaigns auto-retarget anyone who viewed a product page, so any channel appeared to 'share' users. Slides also mixed two percentages with different denominators (union vs per-circle).
actions: Rebuilt campaign grouping as a keyword cascade (streaming first, then purchase/loyalty/consideration, awareness as remainder) and removed hard-coded dates in favour of the console reporting window
Restricted the analysis to DSP only after reasoning that search ads are retargeting by construction
Defined pure incremental rate = channel-only users / channel total and retargeting rate = overlap / source-stage total
Chose four pairwise Venns over a five-set Venn for readability and split overlap share and retargeting flow into two captioned tables
Verified AI estimates against my own Python output and corrected the 62% -> 38.5% misread
Translated my English script to Japanese with a strict 'nothing beyond the source' rule for the client presentation
impact: Client deck concluded streaming formats deliver a low-overlap incremental audience and should be kept at minimum budget while data matures
Retargeting funnel setup validated as working; brand-line finding suggested room to grow therapeutic-line exclusive reach

headline: Rebuilt a time-to-conversion and dayparting query on exposure time so off-peak hours are credited for the sales they generate
context: After Amazon questioned whether a pet nutrition brand's hourly report was based on ad time or purchase time, I re-based the AMC query on traffic time, added hourly buckets, impression hour, day-part and spend.

detail.overview: Converted a conversion-time template to amazon_attributed_events_by_traffic_time, locked the traffic window to one month with a two-month console window so late conversions are captured, restricted to DSP with brand-halo purchases, added campaign-group CTEs with sargable filters, 25 hourly buckets from impression/click to purchase, impression hour and five day-parts, and joined hourly DSP spend for hourly ROAS.
detail.problem: Hourly ROAS keyed on purchase time under-credits off-peak exposure hours. The first runs returned no rows for three overlapping reasons: a wrong year filter, a purchase column that excludes brand-halo sales (most DSP conversions), and confusion over the DSP-only filter. Average time-to-conversion then came back NULL in many buckets because of AMC's 100-user aggregation threshold on timestamp-based fields.
actions: Isolated each no-result cause with diagnostic queries (campaign presence, monthly distribution, ad product type) before changing the main query
Switched the purchase filter to total purchases to include brand-halo conversions and kept DSP-only after confirming the campaign code meant the product line, not sponsored display
Documented the four table-by-time-basis combinations and locked traffic vs conversion windows explicitly
Diagnosed NULL averages as a distinct-user threshold effect (purchases are not users) and removed the average columns rather than report unreliable values
Integrated Amazon's dayparting instructional query: impression hour, day-part and hourly spend
impact: Hourly time-to-conversion query validated against console output; spend-joined hourly ROAS version built but not yet run

headline: Built a reusable AMC reporting pipeline that classifies 100+ Amazon ad campaigns into brand × species × funnel tiers and joins cost to NTB KPIs
context: Monthly Amazon Ads report for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan); I owned the AMC SQL, funnel taxonomy and Excel post-processing.
metrics: Unclassified campaigns driven from 13 to 0 through three diagnostic iterations
DSP vs Sponsored Ads spend split reported as a 67/33 share view per management request

detail.overview: The February monthly report needed cost, NTB revenue/purchases, NTB ratio and AOV for every combination of brand line (wellness / therapeutic), species (dog / cat) and funnel stage, for both DSP and Sponsored Ads, straight out of Amazon Marketing Cloud.
detail.problem: Campaign names were not standardized (mixed separators and ad-hoc tokens), cost and conversion data live in different AMC tables at different grains, and DSP and Sponsored Ads events share one attribution table distinguished only by a nullable product-type column.
actions: Designed a template with injectable VALUES CTEs (campaign IDs, campaign names, target ASINs) that splits DSP and Sponsored Ads via the ad_product_type rule and unions the two KPI sets
Wrote CASE-based string classification (brand line -> species -> sub-funnel -> ACPL roll-up) and a companion diagnostic query that lists every campaign falling into OTHER with the reason
Iterated the rules against real AMC output three times until no campaign was unclassified, adding exceptions for sale, brand-video and ASIN-targeting campaigns
Aggregated cost (dsp_impressions / sponsored_ads_traffic, CPC and vCPM split) and conversions (attributed events) separately with the same classification, then LEFT JOINed on the group keys
Added a campaign-name drill-down level and separated species and sub-funnel into orthogonal columns so downstream Sheets/Python could build segment keys
Handled what AMC could not in Excel: YoY growth, DSP/AMS share columns, exclusion of bonus and zero-cost rows
impact: Delivered the February report with a fully classified campaign set and a reusable query bank for subsequent months
Standardized KPI definitions (AOV = revenue / orders vs ASP = revenue / units) across the report
Flagged an AMC-vs-console click/cost discrepancy for follow-up rather than reporting unreconciled numbers

headline: Built a 2.7k-ASIN competitor list for Amazon Japan conquesting by designing scrape keywords, an auto-classification sheet and a 40-ASIN targeting shortlist
context: Competitor conquesting groundwork for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan); I owned keyword design, the classification rules and the final list handed to the client.
metrics: 89 scrape keywords across 3 product groups designed to avoid therapeutic / wellness overlap
Vendor list (~4k ASINs) plus agency scrape consolidated to ~2.7k in-stock, de-duplicated ASINs
40 targeting ASINs selected as 10 per category with a 3 top / 3 mid / 4 niche mix

detail.overview: The client supplied a list of competitor products mapped to its own four-way taxonomy (therapeutic / wellness × dog / cat) and expected the agency to build a comparable competitor ASIN universe on Amazon Japan, then pick ASINs for Sponsored Products targeting.
detail.problem: Amazon search surfaces the same top sellers repeatedly, so scrape depth alone does not add new ASINs; product titles are unstructured Japanese text with brand-only tokens that span both species; and the client's 'therapeutic' label did not match the literal therapeutic-diet keyword.
actions: Designed Japanese scrape keywords per group (therapeutic must contain a therapeutic-diet token; wellness gets dog/cat suffixes) and excluded the client's own brand terms entirely
Chose a wide-then-deep scrape plan: many keywords at 200–300 results, de-duplicate, then 500+ only for keywords with high unique yield
Built a Google Sheets classifier with a separate keyword tab (partial-match columns, exact-title override columns, TEXTJOIN-generated regex) so rules are maintained by editing rows, not formulas
Iterated the classifier against the client's labeled list, fixing species misclassification with line-code rules (e.g. dog vs cat product codes) and moving ambiguous brands to exact overrides
Normalized scraped brand strings, mapped them to the client taxonomy, flagged unmapped brands as candidates for approval, and merged vendor and agency lists after stock and duplicate checks
Selected 40 targeting ASINs (10 per category) balancing top, mid and niche sellers to avoid bidding only on the most contested products
impact: Delivered the consolidated competitor ASIN list and the targeting shortlist to the client
Identified that therapeutic-line competitor ASINs were under-represented and redirected scraping to three therapeutic brands by species and condition
Surfaced a taxonomy-definition gap (client 'therapeutic' ≠ literal therapeutic diet) for client confirmation before further classification
skills: Regex / LET / IFS in Google Sheets

headline: Reframed a client's 'budget vs NTB correlation' ask into a 3-layer allocation / contribution / relationship view across 5 segment dimensions
context: Quarterly NTB growth review (Dec–Feb) for a global pet nutrition brand (Japan); I designed the analysis frame, the Sheets summary tables and the Python/Looker prototypes.
metrics: Wellness-line cost share fell 79% -> 67% (Dec -> Feb) while its NTB-revenue share held at 46-48%
Search-ads cost share moved 37% -> 57% (Jan -> Feb) with NTB-revenue share 40% -> 67%
Therapeutic line: ~1/3 of spend but over half of NTB revenue in Feb

detail.overview: The client asked what the current budget allocation by funnel was, how NTB contribution compared, and whether investment changes correlated with NTB. I turned this into a three-layer frame — cost share (allocation), NTB revenue/units share (contribution), and month-over-month direction/gap (relationship) — at brand × species × media × funnel × sub-funnel granularity.
detail.problem: Raw data mixed subtotal rows with leaf rows, metric scales differed by 10^4, DSP and search-ads funnels used different naming, one month had duplicate rows, and only three monthly data points existed — far too few to claim a statistical correlation.
actions: Rebuilt a leaf-row-only monthly summary in Sheets (SUMIFS on group keys) and recomputed AOV as sum(revenue)/sum(orders) instead of averaging row-level AOVs
Designed a combo chart: stacked bars for absolute NTB revenue by brand line plus index lines (first month = 100) for cost, revenue and AOV on a secondary axis
Wrote Colab/pandas code that builds a 5-dimension segment key and outputs cost share, NTB revenue share, share gap (NTB share minus cost share) and NTB ROAS heatmaps per month
Prototyped the same view in Looker Studio with CASE-based monthly calculated fields for Dec/Jan/Feb and MoM % columns after discovering DATE_TRUNC is unsupported
Standardized the summary table's change indicators as percentage-point differences with arrow formatting and conditional-format rules driven by source cells
Rewrote the narrative from 'cost fell so NTB fell' to 'NTB revenue declined less than cost, so efficiency improved', supported by NTB ROAS and cost per NTB purchase
impact: Delivered a full-month February view at every level the client asked for, with share, share-gap and MoM columns
Designed the segment-level diagnostic (share gap heatmap) that answers 'which pocket converts budget into NTB best' — execution output not recorded [REVIEW]
Limited correlation claims to directional statements with an explicit note that three months cannot support a strong-correlation conclusion
skills: Google Sheets (SUMIFS, index charts, conditional formatting)

headline: Answered 'how long after ad exposure do users convert?' with an AMC time-to-conversion model that respects the 14-day attribution window and censoring
context: Ad-exposure-to-purchase timing analysis for a premium coffee brand (Japan, machine vs consumable lines, search + DSP); I adapted Amazon's template, redesigned the buckets and defined the cohort cut-offs.
metrics: Bucket design consolidated from 37 to 11 tiers covering the full 14-day attribution window
Campaign filter of 17 IDs restored after finding OR-joined WHERE conditions returned 30+ campaigns

detail.overview: The client asked how long it takes users to convert after seeing an ad. Starting from Amazon's time-to-conversion template, I built a bucketed lag distribution (seconds between impression and conversion) for machine and consumable campaigns across search and DSP.
detail.problem: The template's CASE only bucketed impressions (everything else fell to 'Other'), its WHERE joined product-type and campaign filters with OR, and pooled three months so the largest bucket was '30+ days' — conversions that are not ad-attributed at all under the 14-day window. Recent exposures also lacked a full 14-day follow-up, distorting late buckets.
actions: Fixed the custom-parameter YAML (comment syntax, indentation) and changed the WHERE logic from OR to AND so only the 17 target campaigns were included

Redesigned buckets iteratively — minute/hour tiers kept because most conversions land within minutes, day tiers compressed to 1–3 / 3–7 / 7–10 / 10–14 days — with two-digit prefixes for stable pivot sorting
Excluded lags beyond 14 days in WHERE (not as a CASE label) because they are not ad-attributed sales
Applied a fully-observed cohort rule: impressions up to 14 days before the data end date, conversions up to the end date, keeping the console range open to avoid truncating late conversions
Separated direct purchases from brand-halo total purchases and added new-to-brand conversions as a second measure
Split machine vs consumable campaigns in Sheets via campaign-name rules and planned separate bar charts with a summary view plus a detailed appendix
impact: Delivered a defensible lag distribution methodology; final chart output and machine-vs-consumable figures pending [REVIEW]
Documented why '30+ days' dominated the naive version so the client would not read censored or unattributed lags as real behavior

headline: Extended AMC path-to-purchase to creative type; found Video reached users at ~half the cost but ~5x lower CVR, so budget stayed Static-led
context: A global pet nutrition brand (Japan) asked whether to add budget to Video creatives; I extended the AMC path query to campaign group x creative type, settled the cost basis for cost-per-reach, and delivered Japanese slides and a presentation script.
metrics: Video cost per reach ~0.5x Static on the same awareness line item (wellness line, first-touch cohort)
Video total CVR ~1/5 of Static (0.02% vs 0.10%) and NTB CVR ~1/6 (0.01% vs 0.06%)
Video NTB acquisition cost ~2.6x Static; share of new-to-brand among converters similar (58% vs 61%)
2025 creative mix: Static 36% / Video 11% / REC 48% / Fire TV 5%

detail.overview: Answered 'should Video get more budget?' from a path-to-purchase angle: modified Amazon's validated path-to-conversion query so DSP touchpoints carry a creative type (Static/Video/REC), pivoted paths by first-touch creative, defined cost-per-reach and CPA on a consistent cost basis, and wrote SD/PD insights, V1/V2 budget plans and a Japanese presentation script.
detail.problem: The standard query grouped paths by campaign only, and the same creative ran across many campaigns. Once creative-level paths existed, cost metrics became ambiguous: path cost is any-touch exposure cost, a pure first-touch cost query gave very different numbers, and a metric labelled 'CPA' was actually cost per first-touch unique user. Conclusions also flipped when the therapeutic-line data was corrected.
actions: Confirmed the AMC schema (creative name lives in the 'creative' column; no separate creative table) after a workflow validation error, and replaced the proposed mapping-table join with a CASE on LOWER(creative)
Kept the validated campaign-group mapping CTEs untouched and changed only the DSP output column to CONCAT(campaign_group, '_', creative_type); left Sponsored Ads ungrouped by creative
Wrote a separate first-touch cost-per-reach query (ROW_NUMBER per user) and fixed a LIKE pattern bug that hid the creative split
Settled the cost basis: report 'Path CPR (first-touch cohort)' = any-touch path cost / first-touch unique users, because billed cost accrues on every touch
Relabelled CPU vs purchase CPA, restricted awareness-funnel judgement to first-touch KPIs (NTB share, CVR, CPR, CPA, frequency) and kept last-touch only as a guardrail for the purchase funnel
Produced SD/PD key sentences, V1/V2 allocation options and a natural-language Japanese script, then answered the client's 'is this really path-based?' challenge
impact: Recommended keeping wellness-line Video at its current share with sale-period-only expansion and prioritising Video assets for Fire TV/Prime Video; recommended pausing therapeutic-line awareness/purchase Video in favour of REC/Static (V1) with an LTV check track (V2)
Established a reusable rule set for creative-level path analysis: schema-first, minimal-change query edits, and numerator/denominator attribution consistency in every KPI label

headline: Scored Amazon funnels on first-touch reach KPIs to propose three 2026 budget scenarios summing to 100%
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I turned Amazon's reach/frequency feedback into a funnel scoring model, three budget-mix scenarios and a path-scoring spec for the data team.
metrics: Top-scored awareness funnel proposed 25% -> 30% of budget; Fire TV 4% -> 8% (NTB scenario)
Sales-efficiency scenario: search ads 38% -> 35%, loyalty 6% -> 3%, Fire TV 2% -> 0%, reallocated to consideration/purchase funnels (+8pp)
Highest first-touch NTB contribution funnel: 33% of all NTB purchasers; strongest NTB orientation: 61% of its converters were new-to-brand

detail.overview: Extended a path-to-purchase analysis with the reach/frequency lens Amazon requested: first-touch pivots per funnel (cost per reach, monthly-equivalent frequency, NTB CVR, NTB CPA, NTB share, NTB contribution), a 4-point increment-priority score, three budget scenarios (sales volume / NTB volume / balanced) and a data-team spec defining three path scorecards (A: NTB-oriented, B: sales-volume driver, C: first-touch scalability + last-touch closing).
detail.problem: Six months of accumulated data made frequency incomparable with monthly saturation intuition; volume metrics were mostly a function of budget size; and mixing first-touch and last-touch attribution in one score produced contradictions (a 'closer' cannot be a first-touch metric). Management wanted sales-volume efficiency while the client insisted on protecting the awareness funnel.
actions: Built first-touch and last-touch funnel pivots in Google Sheets and normalised frequency to a monthly equivalent (x 30/180) applied once at the aggregate level
Defined a 4-point increment-priority score (NTB orientation 2pt, CPA below median 1pt, CPR below median 1pt) with frequency as a saturation gate rather than a score
Excluded volume share from the score because it mostly reflects budget size, keeping it as a tie-breaker
Separated roles: first touch = where to grow (CPR/frequency), last touch = where to protect (volume/CPA/ROAS), after finding last-touch was not dominated by search ads
Drafted three 100%-sum scenarios with client constraints applied (keep awareness, cut loyalty and Fire TV, trim search ads) and wrote concise English slide copy
Wrote a data-team spec (definition, formula, why, attribution note) for path scorecards A/B/C with explicit cost-attribution rules and brand-separation requirements
impact: Delivered three budget scenarios aligned to 2026 objectives with a transparent scoring rationale for management and client review
Designed the path-scoring spec and attribution rules for data-team implementation (implementation and incremental-effect validation pending)

headline: Segmented 174 SKUs into 3 new-customer roles; top 20 SKUs held 37% of new-to-brand purchases, shaping the 2026 budget recommendation
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I built the SKU-level new-to-brand portfolio analysis and the client-facing slides for both the wellness and therapeutic lines.
metrics: Top 20 of 174 SKUs = 37% of all new-to-brand purchases
4 derived KPIs (NTB ratio, NTB CAC, total ROAS, NTB contribution) from 1 AMC query
Segment thresholds tuned per line: 40/25% (wellness) vs. 30/20% (therapeutic)

detail.overview: The client asked which SKUs genuinely acquire new customers and where 2026 ad budget should go. Starting from a full-year AMC extract of NTB, total (halo-inclusive) and promoted sales per SKU plus allocated cost, I designed the KPI set, the segmentation rule and a one-slide bubble-chart story per product line.
detail.problem: Ranking by NTB ratio alone surfaced tiny SKUs with high ratios but negligible volume; 174 SKUs could not be shown on one chart; and the wellness-line thresholds produced a lopsided split when reused on the therapeutic line, whose NTB ratios never exceeded 40%.
actions: Added an NTB contribution KPI (SKU NTB purchases / all NTB purchases) as the volume gate before any ratio-based classification
Chose halo-inclusive totals so entry-point SKUs get credit for purchases of other SKUs in the brand
Filtered to the top 20 by contribution, then classified by NTB ratio into three functional groups with plain Japanese labels instead of marketing nicknames
Built the bubble chart (ROAS x NTB ratio, size = contribution, series = segment) and a facts-only English/Japanese recommendation slide
Re-tuned thresholds for the therapeutic line from its observed distribution and rewrote the commentary in the same voice
impact: Delivered the wellness-line Top 15 slide with a clear 2026 direction: shift budget toward the two acquisition-oriented groups
Produced matching therapeutic-line segmentation and commentary; operational translation into DSP/SA targeting is the next step

headline: Re-planned a two-wave spring sale budget by daily-spend density and incrementality floors, shifting the line split from 77:23 to 72.5:27.5
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I audited the client's sale simulation and used my own MMM outputs to design daily budgets per product line and sale wave.
metrics: Daily spend density ~2.2x prior-year March at the same total (14 sale days vs. 31)
April incrementality floor held at ~0.64 (wellness) / >=0.5 (therapeutic) by capping second-wave budget
Line split re-planned 77:23 -> 72.5:27.5 within the same total budget

detail.overview: The client's simulation for a first-ever spring sale used worst-case CTR/CVR/CPC assumptions and fell far short of target, while splitting the budget 50:50 across two waves. With no daily data and no prior spring sale, I had to judge whether the plan would cannibalize organic sales and propose daily budgets by line and wave.
detail.problem: Which benchmark to use for an event that never ran; how to compare a 14-day burst against monthly incrementality ratios; and how to reconcile AI-generated forecasts that contradicted basic diminishing-returns logic.
actions: Rejected the worst-case simulation and benchmarked on the three months where incrementality was proven positive, excluding the saturated summer event
Challenged an unexplained 2.5x sale-day weighting and forced a data-based re-derivation from a normal month vs. a sale month (~2.0x)
