Reframed the client's question from wave totals to daily spend per line, showing the same total compressed into 14 days roughly doubles daily density
Replaced AI-estimated daily spends with actual prior-year daily spends and ratios per line and month
Locked the low-ratio second wave at a defended level and reallocated the remainder to the high-ratio first wave, raising the therapeutic-line share
impact: Designed a daily budget table per line and wave within the same total budget (final sign-off pending in the log)
Gave the client a defensible answer to 'will this cannibalize?' in terms of daily density and ratio floors rather than wave totals

headline: Traced an 81-86% 'existing customer' share in 365-day-excluded awareness campaigns to a targeting-vs-measurement definition gap and framed a binary escalation to Amazon
context: For a global pet nutrition brand (Japan) I handled the manager and client questions on why awareness campaigns excluding recent buyers still reported mostly existing-customer purchases.
metrics: NTB share of purchases 19% (video) / 14% (connected TV) despite 365-day buyer exclusion
2 conflated KPIs separated: impression-based NTB rate vs. purchase-based NTB share
1 binary question (definition YES/NO) replacing an open-ended escalation

detail.overview: Two always-on awareness campaigns (video and connected TV) were targeted with an AMC audience excluding anyone who bought the brand in the last 365 days, yet Amazon's report showed 81-86% of attributed purchases coming from existing customers. My manager and then the client asked how that was possible.
detail.problem: The question mixed two different metrics, the reporting definition of 'existing' was unknown, and the answer could be either our own audience setup error or a definitional gap (e.g. NTB defined as lifetime never-purchased, so lapsed buyers count as existing).
actions: Separated the impression-denominator NTB rate (expected to be tiny for awareness) from the purchase-denominator NTB share (the real anomaly)
Listed candidate causes: brand-halo scope mismatch, audience refresh lag, view-through attribution of loyal buyers, CTV viewer-to-account mapping, and our own audience query
Used elimination logic: if exclusion worked, all 'existing' buyers would be 366+ day lapsed customers, which is implausible for pet food
Wrote a four-part investigation request to Amazon forcing a YES/NO on the 'existing' definition so the reply lands on either a setup fault or a definition gap
Reframed the client's follow-up as a lifetime-definition hypothesis with a lookback-window confirmation request
impact: Designed the escalation so the next step is decidable regardless of Amazon's answer (audit our audience vs. explain lapsed-buyer re-entry)
Gave the manager a clean two-metric explanation for the annual review

headline: Rebuilt a 59-campaign grouped path-to-conversion query through Amazon's AMC query agent and designed a pre/post test for whether a premium DSP campaign type was hijacking last-touch credit
context: For a global PC brand (Japan) I owned the AMC path analysis requested by the media agency partner, across DSP and Sponsored Ads for PC and monitor lines.
metrics: 12 DSP + 47 Sponsored Ads campaigns mapped into 14 path groups
5+ agent-generated query versions reviewed; 8 logic defects caught before execution
1 pre/post design (no-P+ month vs. P+ month) x 2 product lines x 4 last-touch types

detail.overview: The partner agency suspected a premium DSP campaign type looked strong only because it kept appearing as the last touch. I needed a chronological path-by-campaign-group query for PC and monitor lines and a comparison against a period when that campaign type did not run.
detail.problem: The AMC query agent has a 4,000-character input limit and a policy filter that rejects anything resembling audience creation; its generated SQL repeatedly broke path logic (joining on group, alphabetical instead of chronological ordering, inner joins dropping unmapped campaigns, invented column names); and the helper LLM kept rewriting code instead of writing instructions.
actions: Split roles explicitly: the query agent owns schema and syntax, the helper LLM writes instructions and reviews logic only, and I inject campaign ID lists myself
Replaced keyword matching with explicit campaign-name lists and requested a placeholder template to stay under the character limit
Kept the standard template's ROW_NUMBER + NAMED_ROW + ARRAY_SORT ordering rather than an unverified ARRAY_AGG ORDER BY, and reworded the request as aggregate reporting to pass the policy filter

Translated the partner's Japanese request into a testable design: pre vs. post month, PC vs. monitor, last-touch type per purchase, read together with total purchase volume to separate cannibalization from incremental lift
Confirmed touch definitions (DSP = impression, Sponsored Ads = click) and set up SharePoint delivery
impact: Delivered a final grouped path query with full chronological path strings and NTB/cost metrics (execution pending)
Designed the last-touch interception test so the partner's hypothesis can be answered with a control period rather than opinion

headline: Turned a client's cannibalization concern into a monthly incrementality ratio guiding seasonal budgets
context: For a global pet nutrition brand in Japan, I led the Amazon/AMC analytics response to the client marketing lead's belief that rising ad spend was cannibalizing organic sales.
metrics: Ad spend vs organic sales correlation of 0.03 across 13 months
Monthly incrementality ratio ranged from -3.28 to 2.25
Prime Day month ratio 0.50 vs peak-season month 0.97

detail.overview: Diagnosed whether increased Amazon ad spend was eating into organic sales for the wellness and therapeutic lines, and packaged the answer as a client deck with a month-by-month incrementality ratio and seasonal budget guidance.
detail.problem: The client was convinced that flat retail revenue despite higher ad spend proved cannibalization. A simple time series was dominated by seasonality, and a 13-month scatter (correlation 0.03) risked the opposite over-claim that no cannibalization existed at all.
actions: Pulled 13 months of ad-attributed, organic and total sales plus ad spend from AMC and built the derived metrics in a shared sheet
Rejected the 'zero correlation = zero cannibalization' framing after finding months where spend rose and organic fell
Defined Incrementality Ratio = MoM change in total sales / MoM change in ad-attributed sales, with a 1.0 break-even and separate handling for negative-sign months
Split the analysis by brand line (wellness vs therapeutic) and added an organic-delta column so readers could see synergy vs substitution directly
Built stacked-bar and three-metric combo charts in Python and formatted tables in Japanese business units for the client deck
Wrote the conclusion around timing rather than budget size, backed by a three-factor Q&A defence (promotion intensity, product type, competition)
impact: Reframed the client conversation from 'ads are cannibalizing' to 'which months scale and which months defend', enabling a seasonal allocation proposal
Identified the wellness line as the main driver of cannibalization in the Prime Day month, while the therapeutic line stayed resilient
Delivered a reusable monthly incrementality table with status coding that fed the follow-on budget simulator

headline: Modelled ad-spend saturation with Hill curves, then chose an incrementality map for client action
context: For a global pet nutrition brand in Japan, I built the response-curve modelling behind the client's request for an MMM ROI curve, as the agency's Amazon analytics lead.
metrics: Monthly total ROAS fell from a 25.0 peak to 13.6 in the highest-spend month
One of 13 monthly points excluded as a data-collection outlier before refitting

detail.overview: Fitted advertising response curves (log, power, quadratic, Hill) to 13 months of Amazon ad spend and total sales to locate the saturation point, translated the curve into a per-month cut/hold/boost table, and ultimately replaced the curve with an ad-spend vs incrementality-ratio map as the client-facing chart.
detail.problem: The client wanted a curve showing how much sales each budget level would return. With only 13 points, two high-spend months and strong seasonality, a single fitted curve either came out nearly straight or shifted its verdict whenever the target marginal ROAS changed, and its above/below-curve position did not actually say whether to cut or add budget.
actions: Rebuilt the input from month-over-month deltas to raw spend and total sales, since a response curve needs absolute inputs
Iterated log-linear, power, quadratic and Hill-function fits with scipy curve_fit, keeping the Hill form as the industry-standard saturating shape
Paired a sales response curve with a ROAS decay curve so that scale-driven ROAS decline (peak season) could be separated from wasteful decline (deal season)
Removed the first month as a data-collection outlier after showing it depressed the fitted baseline
Converted the curve into a per-month table of saved spend vs lost sales at a 10% cut, replacing above/below-curve reasoning with marginal-efficiency reasoning
Dropped the BCG-matrix framing and the curve itself as the client chart in favour of an ad spend vs incrementality ratio scatter with explicit thresholds
impact: Designed the analytical basis for a seasonal budget shift proposal (defend deal-season months, scale peak-season months)
Established that chart colours must come from the model or the simulator, not hard-coded month lists — a check reused in the follow-on Excel simulator
Curve parameters and per-month gain/loss figures remain unverified against actual outcomes [REVIEW]

headline: Built a client-operated Excel budget simulator that converts monthly incrementality ratios into scale/cut decisions
context: For a global pet nutrition brand in Japan, I designed and iterated an Excel what-if tool so the client marketing team could test monthly Amazon budget changes themselves, as the agency's analytics lead.
metrics: Simulator reproduces actual sales exactly at 0% adjustment (control-total check)
Diminishing returns modelled so that doubling a month's budget halves its incremental efficiency
Peak-month gains flipped from positive at +20% to negative at +30% in the margin-based version

detail.overview: Turned a Python response-curve analysis into a hand-off Excel simulator: the client enters a monthly budget adjustment and sees expected sales, adjusted efficiency and a traffic-light verdict, with the logic evolving from a Hill function to a power law with organic baselines to a direct monthly incrementality-ratio model.
detail.problem: Porting the fitted curve into Excel reversed the analytical story (the deal-season month came out profitable), because the chart colours had been hard-coded and the single curve only reflected spend size, not season. Fixed elasticity and an assumed retail margin then produced verdicts the client could easily challenge.
actions: Set a control-total rule that a 0% adjustment must reproduce actual sales, and used it to reject each broken version
Replaced a fitted baseline with each month's actual organic sales so seasonality entered the model as data rather than a parameter
Applied the month's own incrementality ratio only to the incremental ad sales, then decayed the ratio as adjustment size grew
Removed the assumed retail margin and elasticity constant, keeping expected sales, adjusted ratio and expected ROAS as the only outputs
Designed an asymmetric verdict: budget increases judged on growth (1.0 / 0.5 / 0 thresholds), budget cuts judged on waste avoided
Reduced the client view to six columns with a single yellow input cell and a two-scenario reading guide, and wrote the before/after simulation slides
impact: Delivered a self-serve tool that let the client test scale-up in high-synergy months and modest cuts in cannibalization months without analyst Q&A
Converted the earlier diagnosis into concrete monthly adjustment proposals for the following year's plan
Designed for realism rather than persuasion: forecast values are model-based and not yet validated against actual spend outcomes [REVIEW]

headline: Diagnosed a 43% AMC-vs-report ad sales gap as cross-channel double counting and rebuilt the query
context: For a global pet nutrition brand in Japan, I owned the Amazon Marketing Cloud extraction that fed the cannibalization analysis and had to reconcile it with the client's monthly report, as the agency's AMC analyst.
metrics: Initial AMC ad-attributed sales were 43% above the monthly report for the same month
Scope of ~300 ASINs handled through a single CTE instead of per-ASIN output

detail.overview: Reconciled AMC-derived monthly ad sales, organic sales, NTB and ad cost against the client's reported ad sales, tracing the overstatement to purchases credited to both a DSP view and a sponsored-ads click, and redesigning the extraction as conversion-level deduplicated, step-separated queries.
detail.problem: The first AMC query returned ad sales roughly 1.4x the reported figure for the same month. Fixes suggested by a general-purpose LLM failed on AMC-specific syntax and table logic, an attributed-only rewrite dropped organic sales to zero, and a combined NTB/organic query produced NTB larger than total ad sales.
actions: Decomposed ad sales by ad product type and attribution type to isolate DSP view-through as the dominant, double-counted component
Specified a deduplication rule keyed on the unique conversion event with click-over-view priority and a 14-day window
Switched to a subtraction method (total orders minus deduplicated ad-attributed orders) so organic sales could be derived consistently
Rewrote instructions for the AMC SQL assistant as logical requirements without naming tables, after direct SQL from a general LLM repeatedly hit parser errors
Split the extraction into separate ad-sales and organic-sales queries with spreadsheet-side control totals (click+view = total, DSP+sponsored = total)
impact: Decomposed ad sales came within roughly 3% of the client report after removing view/click double counting [REVIEW: AI-read from result image]
Produced a reusable prompting pattern for AMC's SQL assistant (requirements, not table names) and a three-cause checklist for report-vs-AMC gaps
Final step-separated query results and the cost-unit conversion remain unverified in the log [REVIEW]
